strengths: Practical and well-motivated setting: Adapting retrieval systems to distribution shifts (multilingual, long text, multimodal) without retraining the retriever or regenerating billions of pre-computed embeddings is an important and economically significant problem.

Insightful analysis of similarity vs. ranking rewards: The discovery and demonstration of 'score inflation'—where optimizing raw cosine similarity causes LLMs to generate generic non-discriminative tokens (e.g., 'environment', 'atmosphere') that raise absolute similarity across all images while degrading retrieval accuracy—is a valuable empirical insight.

Broad evaluation across diverse distribution shifts: The empirical validation spans 5 distinct benchmarks representing three major distribution shift scenarios (multilingual on Flickr30k-CN, CVLUE, XM3600; length shift on Wikipedia; multimodal composed retrieval on CIRR) across three CLIP backbones (ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14).
Consistent retrieval gains: GRAPE achieves consistent improvements over both vanilla CLIP and zero-shot LLM rewriting, gaining on average +4.5% R@1 and +4.9% R@10.
weaknesses: Notational errors and typos in core formulations: There are noticeable typos and errors in key parts of the paper. Most notably, the paper title writes 'LET GPRO SUPERVISE' instead of 'GRPO'. In Equation 3, the policy objective is written as $\log \pi_\theta(r_k | q, C)$, where $r_k$ denotes target image rank rather than the generated rewrite $\tilde{q}_k$. Additionally, the abstract abruptly ends with 'The code is available at ' without any URL.

Absence of competitive training baselines: Comparisons are strictly between vanilla CLIP, zero-shot LLM rewriting, and GRAPE. The paper lacks comparisons against supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on available text-image pairs/pseudo-captions, or alternative policy optimization algorithms (e.g., PPO or DPO with ranking pairs).

Unquantified latency and computational overhead: Deploying a 3B or 7B LLM/VLM with reasoning chains (<think>...</think>) before the retrieval stage introduces significant latency overhead in search applications. The paper discusses this qualitatively in Section 5 but provides no empirical measurements of latency, throughput, token generation lengths, or FLOPs.

Ambiguity regarding candidate pool size ($N$) during training: Ranking candidates to compute $r_k$ requires evaluating candidate pool items. The paper does not clarify whether $N$ corresponds to the full dataset training pool (e.g., ~30k images for Flickr30k) or in-batch negative candidates during each training step, leaving the exact computational cost of training ambiguous.

Trivial theoretical contribution in Appendix A.1: The 'proof' in Appendix A.1 simply demonstrates that standard z-score normalization is invariant to affine transformation, which is an elementary property rather than a substantive theoretical finding.

strengths: Practical and timely problem: Enhancing retrieval under distribution shifts without modifying the retriever or re-indexing massive embedding databases is of high practical value.

Insightful analysis of 'score inflation': The paper highlights and empirically illustrates a key pitfall of similarity-based RL optimization—where the model learns to inject generic, high-frequency tokens (e.g., 'environment', 'image') that inflate absolute cosine similarity while degrading relative retrieval ranking.

Comprehensive empirical scope: Evaluated across three distinct distributional shift dimensions (multilingual, long text, and multimodal/CIRR) and three CLIP model scales (ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14), demonstrating consistent gains over zero-shot retrieval and frozen LLM rewriting.
Well-structured presentation and clear qualitative case studies (Figures 2 and 3) explaining why the rewritten queries perform better.
weaknesses: Typo in the central policy objective (Equation 3): The objective writes $\log \pi_\theta(r_k \mid q, C)$ instead of the likelihood of generating the rewritten query $\log \pi_\theta(\tilde{q}_k \mid q, C)$, since $r_k$ denotes the target rank rather than the generated sequence.

Lack of competitive learning-based baselines: The evaluation primarily compares GRAPE against zero-shot prompting (+LLM) and vanilla CLIP. Comparing against standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) using ground-truth caption pairs or other preference optimization techniques (e.g., DPO with hard negatives) would strengthen the empirical claims regarding GRPO's specific advantages.

Missing operational details regarding training-time ranking: For large training pools (e.g., ~30k images in Flickr30k-CN), it is unclear whether rankings $r_k$ are computed against the full training corpus or a sampled in-batch negative set, and how this impacts training throughput.

Inference latency: Relying on a 3B LLM or 7B VLM to rewrite every query before retrieval introduces notable latency overhead in real-time search settings; empirical measurements of generation latency and throughput are absent.

strengths: Practical and timely motivation: Retraining multimodal retrievers like CLIP invalidates pre-computed offline vector indices, making query-side adaptation for frozen embeddings a highly relevant and cost-effective objective.

Insightful analysis of score inflation: The paper clearly identifies and analyzes why directly optimizing cosine similarity via RL fails (i.e., LLMs learn to emit generic tokens that artificially inflate cosine similarity to all candidates without improving discrimination) and demonstrates how ranking-based feedback overcomes this issue.

Broad empirical evaluation: Experiments span multiple distinct distribution-shift settings (multilingual retrieval across many languages, long-form Wikipedia queries, and composed image retrieval on CIRR) across three CLIP backbone scales.
weaknesses: Inadequate baseline comparisons: The main table only compares against zero-shot CLIP and zero-shot LLM rewriting. There are no comparisons against Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) of the LLM rewriter, direct preference optimization (DPO), or existing query rewriting/prompt tuning methods (e.g., PlugIR, ComCLIP, or established frozen-backbone CIR methods on CIRR). It remains unclear whether RL via GRPO outperforms standard supervised adaptation on the training sets.

Limited algorithmic novelty: The framework directly applies existing GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) with a linear mapping of rank as reward. The claimed theoretical proof of affine invariance in Section A.1 is an elementary property of z-score standardization rather than a substantive theoretical contribution.

Ambiguities in training setup and scalability: It is unclear what candidate pool size $N$ is used during training to compute the rank $r_k$. Performing full-corpus retrieval over tens or hundreds of thousands of candidate embeddings for $K$ generated rollouts at every training step would be prohibitively slow, yet the manuscript does not specify whether sub-sampled negatives or in-batch candidates were used.

Lack of inference cost and latency analysis: Using a 3B LLM or 7B VLM to autoregressively rewrite queries adds hundreds of milliseconds of latency to an otherwise millisecond-scale CLIP vector search pipeline. The paper acknowledges this in the discussion but provides no quantitative profiling of latency, FLOPs, or memory footprint.

Notational errors and formatting artifacts: In Equation (3), the policy gradient objective is written as $\log \pi_	heta(r_k \mid q, C)$ rather than over the generated token sequence $	ilde{q}_k$ (where $r_k$ was previously defined as the scalar rank integer). In Section 3.2, the advantage expression has broken formatting, and the abstract ends abruptly with an empty placeholder: 'The code is available at'.

strengths: Practical and timely motivation: adapting queries to frozen multimodal retrievers (such as CLIP) via LLM rewriting avoids the substantial computational overhead of retraining encoders and re-indexing massive vector databases.

Insightful analysis of score inflation: identifying that direct similarity score optimization leads to reward hacking (where generic, non-discriminative words boost absolute similarity across all candidates at the expense of ranking accuracy) is an important finding, and the corpus-relative ranking reward effectively targets this issue.

Comprehensive benchmark coverage across multiple distributional shifts, including multilingual retrieval (Flickr30k-CN, CVLUE, XM3600), long-form queries (Wikipedia), and multimodal composed image retrieval (CIRR).
weaknesses: Severe evidential and credibility concern in baseline evaluations: Table 4 and Section A.3 benchmark against non-existent proprietary models ("Claude-Sonnet-4.6" and "GPT-5.4"). Reporting quantitative metrics for models that do not exist raises substantial concerns regarding the provenance, integrity, and validity of the experimental results.

Critical formulation errors in core methodology: In Equation (3), the policy objective is formulated with log-likelihood $\log \pi_\theta(r_k \mid q, C)$ over the ranking $r_k$, whereas the policy $\pi_\theta$ generates the rewritten query tokens $\tilde{q}_k$. The target ranking $r_k$ is a deterministic/external outcome from CLIP, not a token sequence generated by the policy.

Lack of essential training-based baselines: While the paper compares against zero-shot LLMs and PlugIR, it lacks standard and necessary baselines such as Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on target captions/pseudo-queries, or alternative preference/RL optimization methods (e.g., DPO, PPO with cross-entropy/ranking objectives).

Incomplete manuscript details: The abstract ends abruptly with an unfinished sentence ("The code is available at "), and critical training specifics regarding ranking computation (e.g., whether the candidate set $\mathcal{I}$ during training is computed over mini-batches or the entire gallery) are insufficiently specified given the computational footprint of sampling $K=8$ sequences per step.

strengths: Practical and timely problem formulation: Adapting to query distribution shifts (multilingual, long-form, multimodal) by updating only a query rewriter while keeping the billion-scale retriever and pre-computed index frozen is of significant practical and industrial value.

Insightful analysis of score inflation: The paper clearly identifies and dissects the failure mode of similarity-based reward optimization, demonstrating how pointwise cosine similarity encourages the model to generate generic, non-discriminative padding tokens (e.g., 'environment', 'atmosphere') that boost absolute similarity but harm relative ranking. The proposed corpus-relative ranking reward effectively resolves this issue.

Comprehensive empirical validation: GRAPE is evaluated across five distinct datasets covering three major distribution shift scenarios (multilingual, long-text, multimodal) across three CLIP backbones (ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14), demonstrating consistent improvements in R@1 and R@10.

Detailed analysis and ablations: The manuscript provides useful ablation studies, including data sample efficiency, group size sensitivity, comparisons with larger proprietary LLMs, and qualitative error/case studies.
weaknesses: Missing training compute and latency details: During GRPO training, each query samples $K=8$ candidate rewrites, each of which must be embedded and ranked against a candidate set of size $N$ (up to tens of thousands of images). The paper lacks concrete reporting on training wall-clock time, GPU resources required, and how the retrieval index is handled during training iterations.

Lack of standard learned rewriter baselines: The comparisons are primarily against zero-shot / frozen LLM prompting and PlugIR. An empirical baseline using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on target descriptions or standard RL baselines (e.g., PPO or DPO) would strengthen the claim that GRPO with ranking reward is the superior training paradigm.

Clarification needed on training pool size ($N$): Equation (4) defines the reward using the total number of candidates $N$. It is not fully specified whether $N$ corresponds to the full training corpus, a fixed validation set, or an in-batch candidate pool during each training step, and how this impacts scalability.

Minor notation and typographical issues: In Equation (3), the policy loss objective is written as $\log \pi_\theta(r_k \mid q, C)$ where $r_k$ represents the rank rather than the generated rewrite tokens $\tilde{q}_k$. Additionally, the abstract ends with an incomplete sentence ('The code is available at'), and Table 4 references model names such as 'GPT-5.4' and 'Claude-Sonnet-4.6' which require clarification.

strengths: Practical Problem Formulation: The paper addresses a significant and realistic challenge in industrial retrieval pipelines: adapting to query distributional shifts (multilingual, long-text, and multimodal) without the prohibitive expense of re-embedding the candidate corpus or retraining frozen vision-language encoders.

Insightful Analysis of Score Inflation: The paper clearly identifies and analyzes the failure mode of similarity-based rewards ('score inflation'), demonstrating both theoretically and empirically that naive similarity optimization encourages the generation of generic, non-discriminative tokens that uniformly inflate similarity at the expense of rank accuracy.

Consistent Gains over Prompted Baselines: Across multiple datasets (Flickr30k-CN, CVLUE, XM3600, Wikipedia, CIRR), the proposed GRPO-based adaptation consistently outperforms zero-shot LLM prompting across different CLIP scales (ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14).
Sample Efficiency: The ablation study demonstrates that GRAPE can achieve a large fraction of its full performance with a relatively small number of training queries (e.g., 10k samples).
weaknesses: Critical Technical Error in Policy Objective (Eq. 3): In Equation (3), the policy gradient objective is written as \(\mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K \tilde{A}_k \log \pi_\theta(r_k \mid q, C) \right]\). The LLM policy \(\pi_\theta\) generates the rewritten query sequence \(\tilde{q}_k\), not the scalar rank \(r_k\). Writing the log-likelihood over the rank \(r_k\) under \(\pi_\theta\) is mathematically incorrect and represents a serious technical flaw in the core formulation.

Dubious and Non-Verifiable Baselines: In Table 4, the paper benchmarks against 'Claude-Sonnet-4.6' and 'GPT-5.4'. These do not exist as public, verifiable models. Introducing results from non-existent model versions without documentation, API specifications, or dates raises serious concerns regarding the reliability, validity, and reproducibility of the experimental evaluation.

Absence of Standard Domain Baselines: In Table 1, GRAPE is only compared against frozen CLIP and zero-shot LLM prompting. Crucial, standard domain-specific baselines are missing across all evaluated settings: (1) Multilingual: Machine Translation (e.g., NLLB, MarianMT, Google Translate) + English CLIP, as well as multilingual encoders like mCLIP and AltCLIP; (2) Long-form text: Existing long-text CLIP adaptations (e.g., Long-CLIP, LoTLIP) or standard summarization pipelines; (3) Composed retrieval: Dedicated composed image retrieval methods (e.g., Pic2Word, SEARLE, Baldrati et al.). Without these, it is impossible to evaluate whether query rewriting via GRPO is competitive with established practices.

Non-Standard CIRR Benchmark Evaluation: The authors evaluate CIRR on an arbitrary 80%/20% split containing only 834 validation queries (Table 2), rather than the standard CIRR validation set (4,181 queries) or official test split, and report non-standard metrics (R@1/R@10 instead of R@1, R@5, R_subset). This prevents any direct or meaningful comparison with existing literature.

Naivety of the Linear Rank Reward: The reward function \(R_k^r = 1 - \frac{2(r_k - 1)}{N - 1}\) is purely linear in rank. Because GRPO computes group-relative advantage \(\tilde{A}_k = (R_k - \mu) / \sigma\), affine transformations of rank are invariant (as noted in Appendix A.1), meaning the reward is effectively identical to \(-r_k\) (up to format reward weighting). In retrieval, distinguishing rank 1 from rank 10 is vastly more important than distinguishing rank 1,000 from rank 1,010. The paper neither justifies linear rank over standard ranking metrics (e.g., reciprocal rank \(1/r_k\) or DCG/NDCG) nor benchmarks non-linear alternatives.

Unaddressed Computational Scalability of Training: Computing full corpus ranking \(r_k \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) across \(N\) candidate items for \(K\) generated candidate rewrites per query at every training iteration is computationally expensive when scaling to realistically sized corpora. The paper does not analyze training time complexity or discuss whether in-batch/sampled negatives can approximate the corpus-wide rank.
